core.definition: The Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of three Jewish young men thrown into a furnace for refusing to worship an idol.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BED. The first and third syllables are reduced to schwa and ih, and the final syllable is oh with a hard g in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a name, though within the Daniel story it carries strong associations with courage and faithfulness.
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name, used in Bible study, church and sermons, especially when discussing Daniel 3. Americans rarely use it outside Scripture. In church settings it usually appears together with Shadrach and Meshach.

examples.everyday: My kids love the story of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the fiery furnace.
examples.professional: In the children's ministry curriculum, Abednego is introduced in the lesson on faithfulness under pressure.
examples.analytical: Daniel 3 presents Abednego as one of three young men whose refusal to worship the golden image is the basis of the narrative's theological argument for trust in God.

nuance.analogy: Like a team member who holds firm when the whole group pressures them to give in.
nuance.etymology: Babylonian name given to Azariah, probably meaning servant of Nebo, a Babylonian god.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Pronouncing the last syllable as neg; it is nih-goh with a hard g.
nuance.biblical_note: Abednego was the Babylonian name given to Azariah, meaning Yahweh has helped in Hebrew, when he was taken into the service of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 1:7). He and his companions Shadrach and Meshach refused to bow to the golden image, trusting God to deliver them, and were thrown into the furnace (Daniel 3:12-18). The king later promoted them in Babylon after their deliverance (Daniel 3:30).

core.definition: A name borne by several men in the Bible, most notably a Levite in Kiriath-jearim who kept the ark of the covenant in his house, and a son of Jesse.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIN, and the last syllable rhymes with 'cab'. The middle vowel is reduced to 'uh', so do not say 'ah-bih-NAH-dab'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name used for biblical people, and Americans mention it mostly in Bible study or in discussions of the ark of the covenant. It is not used as a modern given name, so it would only come up in religious or historical contexts.

examples.everyday: In Bible study, we learned that Abinadab kept the ark in his house for twenty years.
examples.professional: For the lesson on the ark, I included Abinadab's house in Kiriath-jearim as the place where the ark rested before David moved it.
examples.analytical: The reference to Abinadab's house in 1 Samuel 7:1 emphasizes the role of a private household in the custody of sacred objects during the period of the judges.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Avinadav', usually understood as 'my father is noble' or 'my father is generous'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the Levite Abinadab with the son of Jesse or the son of Saul, who are different people.
Stressing the middle syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Abinadab (Hebrew Avinadav) is borne by several men in the Old Testament. 1 Samuel 7:1 says the ark of the covenant was taken to the house of Abinadab on the hill in Kiriath-jearim, where his son Eleazar was set apart to keep it. 2 Samuel 6:3-4 describes the ark being carried from his house when David brought it to Jerusalem. 1 Samuel 16:8 names a son of Jesse, and 1 Samuel 31:2 names a son of Saul who died in battle at Gilboa.

senses.definition: First according to historical or scientific records; original; indigenous; primitive.
Living in a land before colonization by foreigners.
An animal or plant native to a region.

core.definition: Original to a place, or relating to the Indigenous people who lived there before colonization. Capitalized, it refers especially to Australia's Aboriginal peoples.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on RIJ, the third syllable. The 'j' sound is like 'juh', and the final syllable is a weak 'nul'. The r is strongly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Potentially sensitive. The word can sound outdated or insensitive when used for Native Americans, and it has specific meaning in Australia.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'Indigenous' or 'Native American' is the preferred term for Native peoples of the United States. 'Aboriginal' is mainly used for Australia's First Nations peoples, with a capital A. Using lowercase 'aboriginal' for animals and plants is technical and rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Indigenous is the preferred and more general term for original inhabitants in American and academic contexts.
Native is common and neutral for things that originate in a place, such as native plants; aboriginal is more formal and historical.

examples.everyday: My friend took a trip to Australia and visited an aboriginal art gallery near Sydney.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit partners with aboriginal communities in Canada, and every project starts with their consent.
examples.analytical: The author questions whether the term aboriginal, with its colonial history, can ever describe peoples without implying a lesser claim to the land.

nuance.analogy: Aboriginal describes something that has been there from the very beginning, like the first trees in a forest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aborigines, 'original inhabitants', from ab origine, 'from the beginning'.
common_mistakes: Using 'aboriginal' for Native Americans in the United States, where 'Native American' or 'Indigenous' is preferred.
Forgetting the capital A when referring to Australia's Aboriginal peoples.

senses.definition: The act or process of cutting off.
A figure of speech employed when a speaker having begun to say a thing stops abruptly.
The natural separation of a part at a predetermined location, such as a leaf at the base of the petiole.

core.definition: The natural shedding of a leaf, flower, or fruit from a plant at a specialized break point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SISH, the second syllable. The final syllable is a syllabic n, so it sounds like 'un' with the n as the main sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise biological term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'abscission' mainly in botany, plant biology, and agriculture classes or reports. In everyday conversation, people say 'leaves falling' or 'leaf drop'. The term is precise but rarely used outside science settings.

distinctions.note: Shedding is a general word for losing parts, while abscission is the specific biological process at a designated layer.
Senescence means the aging of the whole plant or organ, while abscission is the separation of a particular part.

examples.everyday: The maple in our yard is dropping all its leaves now, and the botanist said that's just abscission.
examples.professional: The orchard trial showed that early fruit abscission cut the yield by about fifteen percent in the second season.
examples.analytical: Abscission reveals how a plant balances resource conservation against the cost of keeping damaged organs, since the separation is controlled by hormones rather than simple decay.

nuance.analogy: Like a perforated page that tears cleanly along a line built in for that purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abscissio, meaning a cutting off, from abscindere, to cut off.
common_mistakes: Confusing abscission with abscissa, the mathematical x-coordinate.
Stressing the first syllable instead of SISH.

abscission.etymology: From Latin *abscissiō*, from *abscindō* (“to cut, to tear”).

senses.definition: To increase, to rise.
To reach or come to by way of increase; to arise or spring up because of growth or result, especially as the produce of money lent.
senses.example: Environmental benefits that accrue to the area.

senses.definition: To be incurred as a result of the passage of time.
senses.example: The monthly financial statements show all the actual but only some of the accrued expenses.

senses.definition: To accumulate.
senses.example: He has accrued nine sick days.

senses.definition: To become an enforceable and permanent right.

core.definition: To gradually build up or grow over time, especially money, interest, benefits or obligations that come to you without active effort.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'kroo', which rhymes with 'crew'. Don't add an extra 'k' or 'sh' sound at the end; the double c is pronounced like a single k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a steady, usually positive gain, such as interest or vacation time, but it carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'accrue' in casual talk; they say 'build up' or 'pile up' instead. You will hear it mostly in work, finance, benefits and legal contexts, such as 'vacation days accrue each month.' In conversation, a natural reply might be 'Oh, good, so the time keeps adding up?'

distinctions.note: Accrue focuses on what you gain by right or through time passing, like interest or benefits. Accumulate focuses on a growing pile of things gathered together.
Gain is general and often active, as in 'gain weight' or 'gain experience.' Accrue suggests a quiet, automatic buildup, often measured in a formal record.

examples.everyday: The interest on that savings account accrues every month, so you'll see a little more money each time you check.
examples.professional: Our PTO accrues at 1.5 days per month, so check your balance before you book that trip to Denver.
examples.analytical: Over time, obligations accrue to a citizen, and those obligations shape what the community can rightly ask of them.

nuance.analogy: Like snow quietly building up on a porch railing overnight, the benefit grows without anyone scooping it up.
nuance.etymology: From Old French acreue, from acreistre, meaning 'to increase,' from Latin accrescere, 'to grow toward.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'acrue' with only one c.
Using 'accrue' for active gathering; for objects you collect on purpose, use 'accumulate' or 'collect.'
Writing 'accrue of' instead of 'accrue to' when a benefit goes to someone.

senses.definition: A process by which the culture of a society changes on contact with a different one.
A process by which a person acquires the culture of the society that they inhabit, starting at birth.

core.definition: The process by which a person or group adopts the customs, language and values of a different culture they come into contact with.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'ray,' with a lighter stress on 'kul.' The 't' before 'ch' merges into a 'ch' sound, so say 'kul-chuh' rather than 'kuhl-too-ruh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term from social science, with no praise or blame attached, though it can be used sensitively or politically in debates about immigration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'acculturation' mostly in sociology, anthropology, education and immigration discussions. In everyday speech they would more often say 'getting used to American life' or 'adjusting to the culture.' Used in conversation, it can sound academic, so a plainer phrase is often better.

distinctions.note: Assimilation implies fuller absorption into the dominant culture, often losing the original identity. Acculturation describes the adjustment process and can keep elements of the original culture.
Enculturation is learning your own culture from childhood. Acculturation is adopting a new culture later in life.

examples.everyday: It took my parents years to pick up American habits, so the whole acculturation thing was harder than they expected.
examples.professional: Our onboarding program covers acculturation to the company's culture across our Chicago and Austin offices, not just the technical training.
examples.analytical: Berry's model of acculturation distinguishes integration, assimilation, separation and marginalization as strategies that groups adopt when they meet a new society.

nuance.analogy: Like a new hire gradually learning the unwritten rules of a team, a person slowly picks up the habits and expectations of a new community.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'culture' with the prefix ad-, and first used in American anthropology in the 1880s.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'culture shock,' which is the feeling of disorientation rather than the process itself.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'uh-kul-cha-RAY-shun' with extra syllables, instead of 'uh-kul-chuh-RAY-shun.'
Using 'acculturation' for everyday small adjustments; it usually refers to a larger group or long-term change.

senses.definition: Synonym of ace up one's sleeve.
senses.example: Our ace in the hole left our opponents stupefied; it isn't every day that an NBA star plays street basketball.

core.definition: A secret advantage or backup plan that you keep in reserve and use when you really need it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'hole,' and 'ace' has a lighter stress. Say 'in thuh' quickly, with 'the' reduced to 'thuh,' and link 'ace in' so it sounds like 'ays-in.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a hidden strength that can save the situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom casually in sports, business, politics and everyday planning, such as 'Our ace in the hole is the new client list.' It is informal but not rude. A natural reply is 'Good, let's keep that in our back pocket.'

distinctions.note: These are near-identical in meaning. 'Ace up one's sleeve' is slightly more common in writing, while 'ace in the hole' is also common in speech.
A trump card is a decisive advantage played at a critical moment. An ace in the hole is more likely to be kept hidden until needed.

collocations: have an ace in the hole
play your ace in the hole
keep an ace in the hole

examples.everyday: My sister always keeps a spare battery in her bag, so she's got an ace in the hole for dead phones.
examples.professional: Our ace in the hole for the renewal is the usage data showing a thirty percent increase in active users.
examples.analytical: A prudent negotiator keeps an ace in the hole, a concession held back until the other side reveals its own limits.

nuance.analogy: Like a card hidden face down in a poker hand, the advantage is kept out of sight until the right moment.
nuance.etymology: From card games such as stud poker, where a card dealt face down is called the hole card.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ace on the hole' instead of 'ace in the hole.'
Using it for a literal card in a deck, since it is a fixed phrase.
Stressing 'in' or 'the' too strongly; they are reduced in speech.

ace-in-the-hole.etymology: From stud poker in which there is one unknown card called the hole card, referring to the optimum hole card being an ace.

conversation.text: Our ace in the hole is the pilot data from the Chicago stores.
If the client pushes back on price, Mike's demo is our ace in the hole.
My grandma's lasagna is my ace in the hole for every potluck.

senses.definition: To misbehave; to cause trouble.
senses.example: My allergies act up during hay fever season.

senses.definition: To perform the duties of an appointment senior to that actually held; to deputize for a superior.
senses.example: Acting up is always recommended when you find yourself under a new boss.

core.definition: To misbehave, or to stop working properly. Used for people, children, pets, cars, machines, and body parts that hurt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on UP, the particle, not on ACT. In fast speech the t in act often links into the u of up, so it sounds like 'ak-TUP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes a problem without blame, so it is gentler than 'misbehave' or 'break'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'act up' constantly for kids, dogs, cars, computers, and aching joints, usually in casual talk. Saying 'My knee is acting up' is natural, and so is 'The printer is acting up again.' For a formal report, use 'malfunction' or 'behave inappropriately' instead. A natural reply is 'Oh no, what's it doing?' or 'Have you tried restarting it?'

distinctions.note: 'Misbehave' is about bad conduct by people, especially children. 'Act up' also covers machines and body parts, and it sounds more casual.
'Malfunction' is formal and technical for equipment that fails. 'Act up' is what you say about the same problem in everyday conversation.
'Play up' is mainly British and Australian for misbehaving or aggravating a condition. Americans say 'act up' instead.

collocations: the kids acted up at dinner
my knee acts up when it rains

examples.everyday: My car has been acting up again, so I'm taking it to the shop on Saturday.
examples.professional: The build server keeps acting up on Fridays, so let's open a ticket with infrastructure.
examples.analytical: A model that acts up under distribution shift reveals fragility in its training, not malice in its design.

nuance.analogy: Like a old appliance that works fine until someone is watching, then starts making noise.
common_mistakes: Using 'act up' for a deliberate, serious wrongdoing by an adult; 'commit fraud' or 'behave badly' fits better.
Saying 'act up to' or 'act up on' instead of simply 'act up'.
Stressing ACT instead of UP, which makes the phrasal verb sound like a noun.

conversation.text: The kids always act up when they're tired and hungry.
Sorry, my dog is acting up because there's a stranger at the door.
My laptop's been acting up all week, so I'm taking it in tomorrow.
My back is acting up again, so I'm skipping the gym today.
The Wi-Fi is acting up again.
My knee always acts up when it rains.

senses.definition: To make great; to enlarge; to increase.
senses.example: to aggrandize one's authority, distress

senses.definition: To make great or greater in power, rank, honor, or wealth (applied to persons, countries, etc.).
To make appear great or greater; to exalt.
senses.example: aggrandize one's accomplishments and downplay others'

senses.definition: To increase or become great.

core.definition: To make someone or something greater in power, status, or wealth, often in a self-serving way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GRAN, the first full syllable after the weak first syllable. The ending -ize is pronounced like 'eyes', not 'eye-zee'.

nuance.connotation: negative or neutral. It often implies that someone is increasing their own power or image for selfish reasons, though it can be neutral when describing a country's growth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in politics, business, and history to describe someone gaining power or status, usually with a hint of self-interest. In casual conversation they say 'build yourself up' or 'make yourself look good'. It can sound stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: 'Enlarge' is a neutral word for making something bigger in size or scope, while 'aggrandize' concerns power, status, or wealth.
'Exalt' means to praise or raise someone to a high position, often with admiration; 'aggrandize' can imply that the increase is excessive or self-serving.
'Magnify' can mean to exaggerate or enlarge an image, while 'aggrandize' focuses on rising in power or importance.

examples.everyday: He keeps telling everyone about his trips to make himself look more important.
examples.professional: Her project summary tends to aggrandize her role, so please check with the team before we share it with leadership.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that the empire aggrandized itself by absorbing its neighbors' territories and resources over several decades.

nuance.analogy: Like a salesman who inflates a small deal into a big one to look more successful.
nuance.etymology: From French agrandir, from a- 'to' plus grand 'great', from Latin grandis.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'aggrandize' with 'aggravate', which means to make worse or to annoy.
Stressing the first syllable as 'AG-ruh-dize' instead of the main stress on GRAN.

senses.definition: The sufferings of Jesus Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane (often capitalized).
Extreme pain or anguish.
senses.example: When the weight fell on her foot, she cried out in agony.

senses.definition: The last struggle of life; death struggle.
Violent contest or striving.
Paroxysm of joy; keen emotion.

core.definition: Intense physical or mental pain, or severe anguish, especially a period of suffering that feels unbearable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to 'uh,' so the word has three syllables and ends in 'nee,' not 'oh-nee.'

nuance.connotation: negative: it describes severe suffering, though Americans often use it hyperbolically for mild frustration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'in agony' for serious pain, and they use the word jokingly for something tedious, such as 'It was agony waiting in line.' Used for physical pain, it is strong, so a simple 'it hurts' is often more natural in a doctor's office. The sense of Jesus' suffering in Gethsemane is capitalized and is mainly a religious use.

distinctions.note: Anguish is deeper emotional suffering, often grief or distress, while agony can describe physical or emotional pain.
Pain is the general word for discomfort or hurt, while agony is stronger and more intense.
Torment usually involves someone or something causing ongoing suffering, while agony describes the suffering itself.

examples.everyday: My back was in agony after I carried the boxes up the stairs, so I lay down on the floor for an hour.
examples.professional: The migration freeze was agony for the team, because every release had to wait for the final approval.
examples.analytical: The Psalmist describes the agony of abandonment as a state in which prayer itself seems to go unanswered.

nuance.analogy: Agony is like a tightening rope, where the pain grows until it feels like a struggle you cannot stop.
nuance.etymology: From Greek agōnia, struggle or contest, from agōn, contest or competition.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as 'ah-GONE-ee,' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Using agony to describe a mild discomfort without the exaggeration that Americans expect, which can sound odd in a formal setting.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word agōnia (ἀγωνία) appears in Luke 22:44 (RSV), which describes Jesus praying in agony in the Garden of Gethsemane before his arrest. Matthew 26:36-46 and Luke 22:39-46 (RSV) tell the same story of Jesus' anguish and prayer before his death. The word emphasizes intense inner struggle, not only physical pain, and is central to the traditional Christian reflection on Christ's suffering.

agony.etymology: 14th century, via Old French and Latin from Ancient Greek *ἀγωνία* (“emulation, competition, struggle”), from *ἀγών* (“contest”).

core.definition: Priest at Nob who gave David holy bread and Goliath's sword; Saul later had him and his priests killed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEL, the third syllable, while the first and last syllables are quick and light. End with a crisp k sound and no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a proper name, used in discussions of the Bible and David's flight from Saul.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly encounter this name in Bible study, especially 1 Samuel, where it refers to the priest at Nob. Say it as a plain name, and add 'the priest at Nob' if your listener might confuse him with others. Do not confuse it with Abimelech, a king in Genesis.

distinctions.note: Abimelech is a king of Gerar in Genesis, while Ahimelech is a priest in Samuel; the names look alike but refer to different people.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader told us about Ahimelech, who gave David bread when he was hungry.
examples.professional: In my class on 1 Samuel, I use the priest Ahimelech to show how David's flight affected the people who helped him.
examples.analytical: The account of Ahimelech in 1 Samuel 21 raises questions about priestly mercy, David's deception, and the cost of loyalty under a jealous king.

nuance.analogy: Like a pastor who opens the church pantry to a traveling stranger, only to be punished for it by a jealous ruler, Ahimelech acts in good faith and pays the price.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Ahimelech, meaning 'my brother is king', from 'ach' (brother) and 'melech' (king).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable and saying AH-hih-mel-ek.
Confusing him with Abimelech, a king in Genesis.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Ahimelech' (אֲחִימֶלֶךְ), meaning 'my brother is king'. Key passages: 1 Samuel 21:1-9 tells how Ahimelech gave David the holy bread and Goliath's sword at Nob; 1 Samuel 22:9-19 reports Doeg the Edomite's testimony to Saul and the killing of Ahimelech and the other priests at Nob; 1 Samuel 26:6 names a Hittite called Ahimelech who went down with David into Saul's camp.

senses.definition: An algorithm for pruning a search tree by eliminating any branch that is demonstrably inferior to a branch previously encountered.

core.definition: A search method that skips parts of a game tree that cannot change the best move, so the computer searches faster and still finds the same best move.

pronunciation.tip: Say AL-fuh, not AL-fah, and keep the reduced vowel in the middle syllables. The main stress falls on PRUN in pruning, and the r is strong and rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term of art with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mainly in computer science, AI courses, and conversations about game engines such as chess programs. You will rarely hear it in everyday talk. In a technical meeting, a natural response is to ask whether it is combined with minimax or with a move-ordering heuristic.

distinctions.note: Minimax searches the whole game tree, while alpha-beta pruning is an optimization of minimax that gives the same answer with less work.
Alpha-beta pruning is exact and guarantees the same result as full search, whereas a heuristic search may skip good moves to save time.

examples.everyday: My friend who builds chess apps said they use alpha-beta pruning so the computer can think faster.
examples.professional: Before we increase the search depth, let's add alpha-beta pruning so the engine stays under the time limit.
examples.analytical: Alpha-beta pruning preserves the minimax value while discarding branches that provably cannot affect the final decision.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player who stops analyzing a line as soon as one reply shows it is clearly worse.
nuance.etymology: Alpha and beta name the two bounds the search tracks, and prune comes from Middle English prunen, to trim.
common_mistakes: Saying AL-fah instead of AL-fuh
Thinking the method can change the result, when it only skips work that cannot matter
Calling it a data structure instead of an algorithm

conversation.text: Alpha-beta pruning skips branches of the minimax tree that can't change the final decision.
With good move ordering, alpha-beta pruning lets the search go roughly twice as deep in the same time.
Alpha-beta pruning returns exactly the same move as plain minimax, just faster.

senses.definition: That which annoys.
senses.example: Having to wait 45 minutes for the bus is a real annoyance, but it's the only way to get to work.

senses.definition: An act or instance of annoying.
The psychological state of being annoyed or irritated.
senses.example: feeling mild annoyance

core.definition: Something that irritates you, or the mild feeling of being irritated by something small and unwanted.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOY, which is the oy diphthong like the vowel in boy. The final -ance is a reduced uhns, not a full ance syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild. It describes small irritations rather than serious anger, so it is common in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use annoyance for small, persistent irritations, such as noise or delays, and often say a minor annoyance or a real annoyance. It is neutral in tone and suits casual and professional speech alike. For a person who irritates you, say an annoying person or a nuisance.

distinctions.note: Irritation often feels sharper or more physical, like a rash; annoyance is milder and more about things getting in your way.
Anger is stronger and more intense; annoyance is a smaller frustration.
A nuisance is the thing or person causing the problem; annoyance is the feeling it produces.

examples.everyday: The constant beeping of the microwave is a minor annoyance, but I got used to it.
examples.professional: Frequent pop-up alerts are an annoyance for users, so we should batch the notifications.
examples.analytical: Philosophers often distinguish between harm and mere annoyance, since something that annoys us may not wrong us at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a pebble in your shoe: small, constant, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From the verb annoy, from Old French anoier, from Latin in odio 'in hatred'.
common_mistakes: Using annoyance to describe a person; say an annoying person or a nuisance.
Spelling it annoyence, with the wrong ending.

annoyance.etymology: Middle English *anoyaunce* (rare form of *noyaunce*), from Old French *anuiance*, *anoiance*, from the verb *anuier* (“to cause problems”), equivalent to *annoy* + *ance*.

senses.definition: The region in a plane between two concentric circles of different radii.
Any topological space homeomorphic to the region in a plane between two concentric circles of different radii.
A ring- or donut-shaped area, object, or structure.
The membranous remnants of a partial veil which leaves a ring on the stem of a mushroom.

A dark ring on a fish's scale that is formed when a fish's growth rate slows down in the winter due to low food intake and the scale's circuli move closer to one another. The dark ring is used to estimate the fish's age, approximately one year per annulus.
In a well such as an oil well or water well: the space between a pipe or tube and any pipe, tube, casing, or sides of a hole surrounding it.

A ring of fibrous tissue; specifically, such a ring around an opening of a heart valve, to which the valve leaflets and muscle fibres of the atria and ventricles are attached; an annulus fibrosus cordis.

A ring of light in a celestial body, especially when caused by an annular eclipse (for example, when the Sun and Moon are in line with the Earth, but the Moon does not completely cover the Sun's disc).

A structure surrounding a sporangium (or part of it) which shrinks and causes it to rupture for spore dispersal; specifically, in a fern: a structure around about two-thirds of the sporangium consisting of differentially thick-walled cells which dry and distort the sporangium; and in a moss: a complete ring of cells around the tip of the sporangium which dissolves to cause the tip to detach.

core.definition: A flat ring-shaped region bounded by two concentric circles of different sizes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AN, and reduce the middle vowel to a quick schwa, so the word has three syllables. Don't add an extra 'oo' sound after the n; say it as 'AN-yuh-lus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is used as a neutral description of shape.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use annulus mainly in mathematics, engineering, biology, and physics, where a precise name for a ring shape is useful. In everyday talk people say ring, donut shape, or circular band instead. In technical writing you will see annulus paired with the adjective annular.

distinctions.note: Ring is a general everyday word, while annulus is a precise geometric or structural term.
A disk is a solid circle with no hole, while an annulus has a hole in the middle.

examples.everyday: The cake came out as a thin annulus, so the middle was completely hollow.
examples.professional: To get the area, compute the outer circle's area and subtract the inner circle's area from it, since that gives the annulus.
examples.analytical: The annulus is a useful model in fluid dynamics because flow between concentric cylinders reduces to a radial problem.

nuance.analogy: An annulus is like the flat part of a bagel's outline when you look straight down at it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin annulus, 'small ring,' a diminutive of anulus, 'ring.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun annulus with the adjective annular; say 'an annular region' but 'an annulus.'
Saying 'an-yoo-lus' with a long u, which sounds unnatural to Americans.

core.definition: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who persecuted Jews and desecrated the Jerusalem Temple, prompting the Maccabean revolt in the second century B.C.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TY, which rhymes with 'eye'. The last two syllables reduce to 'uh-kus'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative in Jewish and Christian tradition, since he is remembered as a persecutor and a type of tyranny.
nuance.usage_note: Used in biblical studies, history and Jewish tradition, especially in connection with Hanukkah. Several Seleucid kings had this name, so specify 'Antiochus IV' or 'Antiochus Epiphanes'.

distinctions.note: Antioch is a city (in Syria, now Turkey); Antiochus is a king's name.
Antiochus III the Great was the father of Antiochus IV and conquered Judea but did not persecute the Jews.
Nebuchadnezzar was a Babylonian king who destroyed the first Temple; Antiochus desecrated the second Temple.

examples.everyday: At the Hanukkah dinner, our host explained how the Maccabees fought against Antiochus.
examples.professional: The course covers the Maccabean period, beginning with Antiochus IV and the crisis in Jerusalem.
examples.analytical: Many scholars read the 'little horn' in Daniel 8 as a reference to Antiochus Epiphanes.

nuance.etymology: From Greek Antiochos, a royal name of the Seleucid dynasty, said to derive from the name Antiochus, father of Seleucus I.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; say an-TY-uh-kus.
Confusing him with the city Antioch.
nuance.biblical_note: Antiochus IV is not named in the RSV Protestant canon but is widely understood to be alluded to in Daniel 8 and 11. He is named in 1 Maccabees 1 and 2 Maccabees 4-9, which describe his plundering of the Temple, the 'abomination of desolation' and the persecution of the faithful. Daniel 11:31 speaks of forces that profane the sanctuary and set up the abomination that makes desolate.

senses.definition: Unwilling or unable to cooperate and associate normally with other people.
senses.example: antisocial person

senses.definition: Antagonistic, hostile, or unfriendly toward others; menacing.
Opposed to social order or the principles of society; hostile toward society.
senses.example: antisocial ideals

senses.definition: Introverted; shy.
An antisocial individual.

core.definition: Not wanting to spend time with other people, or behaving in ways that are hostile toward others or that harm society.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SO, and the ending is a reduced schwa, so say it as 'shul,' not 'shul' with a full vowel. Learners often stress the first syllable, which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: negative in most contexts. It is milder in casual speech, where people may joke that they feel antisocial and want to stay home.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'antisocial' often means someone who avoids people or doesn't enjoy parties, and people say 'I'm feeling a little antisocial today' to mean they want to be alone. In legal, psychological, or news contexts, 'antisocial behavior' means conduct that harms others or society. It sounds a bit clinical when describing a friend, so 'not very social' or 'keeps to himself' is softer.

distinctions.note: Shy describes discomfort around people. Antisocial suggests a deliberate choice to avoid people or hostility toward them.
Unsociable is milder and only means not friendly or talkative. Antisocial can also mean hostile or harmful.
Introverted is a neutral personality trait. Antisocial implies avoidance that others find troubling or, in a legal sense, harmful conduct.

examples.everyday: Don't invite me tonight, I'm feeling kind of antisocial and just want to watch TV.
examples.professional: HR flagged the antisocial behavior in the meeting, where he kept interrupting and ignoring everyone's questions.
examples.analytical: Durkheim treats antisocial acts as behavior that breaks the shared norms a society needs in order to hold together.

nuance.analogy: An antisocial person is like a solo instrument that refuses to join the orchestra, either by staying silent or by playing against the others.
nuance.etymology: From anti- (against) plus social, from Latin socialis, 'allied,' from socius, 'companion.'
common_mistakes: Using antisocial to mean 'against social media' or 'opposed to social causes' in everyday conversation.
Confusing it with asocial, which means not interested in social interaction at all, without the hostility.

senses.definition: Tending to doubt.

core.definition: Involving or expressing doubt, puzzlement, or an unresolved logical difficulty, especially in an argument or philosophical dialogue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, RET, and the first vowel is a short 'a' as in 'cat'. Keep the 'r' rhotic, and do not add an extra syllable between the 'p' and the 'r'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in philosophy, and it sounds specialized outside that field.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aporetic almost only in philosophy and classics, especially for Socratic dialogues that end without a firm conclusion. In normal conversation, people say 'unresolved' or 'puzzling' instead. It describes a dialogue, text, or argument, not a person's feelings, so say 'doubtful' or 'uncertain' for people.

distinctions.note: Skeptical describes a habit of doubting claims, while aporetic describes an argument or dialogue that reaches an unresolved puzzle.
Doubtful is common and personal; aporetic is technical and describes a question or argument rather than a feeling.
Inconclusive means no clear result was reached; aporetic adds that the puzzle is built into the question itself.

collocations: the aporetic character of the argument

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor said the book ends in an aporetic way, and I still can't tell you what the author actually thinks.
examples.professional: Our review notes say the policy memo leaves the central trade-off aporetic, so we need a clearer decision before we ship.
examples.analytical: Plato's early dialogues often end aporetically, leaving Socrates and his interlocutor with a sharpened question rather than a settled doctrine.

nuance.analogy: An aporetic argument is like a maze whose paths all loop back to the entrance: each route looks open but none leads to a final answer.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aporetikos, 'doubting, puzzled', from aporein, 'to be at a loss', from a- 'without' and poros 'passage'.
common_mistakes: Using aporetic to describe a doubtful person rather than an argument or text.
Confusing aporetic with apophatic, which is unrelated in meaning.

aporetic.etymology: From French *aporétique*, from Ancient Greek *ἀπορητικός*, from *ἄπορος*.

senses.definition: To agree to a proposal.
Agreement; act of agreeing.
senses.example: I will give this act my assent.

senses.definition: A legal instrument that conveys real estate to an heir under the terms of a will.

core.definition: To agree to something, especially a proposal, request, or formal decision, often after consideration.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, SENT, and the 't' is a clear final sound. Learners sometimes stress the first syllable or confuse the vowel with 'ascent,' which has a different meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals formal approval rather than enthusiasm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'assent' mostly in formal, legal, or political writing, such as 'The governor assented to the bill.' In daily speech people say 'agree,' 'go along with,' or 'say yes.' If you say 'I assent' in a casual office conversation, it may sound stiff or overly formal.

distinctions.note: 'Agree' is everyday and general; 'assent' is more formal and often implies a formal approval or acceptance of a proposal.
'Consent' often refers to permission, especially in legal or personal matters; 'assent' is more about agreeing to a proposal or statement.

examples.everyday: My landlord finally assented to fixing the heater after I sent three emails.
examples.professional: The committee assented to the timeline, but only after the security team signed off.
examples.analytical: A reader may assent to an argument intellectually without yet being persuaded to act on it.

nuance.analogy: Like nodding your head in a meeting when someone makes a point you accept.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'assentire,' to agree, from 'ad-' and 'sentire' to feel or think.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'assent' with 'ascent,' which means going upward.
Using 'assent to' with a person as if it means 'agree with the person'; it usually refers to a proposal or decision.

assent.etymology: From Middle English *assent* and *assenten*, from Old French *assent* and *assentir*, from Latin *assentiō* (whence *as-*).

senses.definition: Not symmetric.
senses.example: an asymmetric shape

senses.definition: Not involving a mutual exchange of keys between the sender and receiver.
Of a relation R on a set S: having the property that for any two elements of S (not necessarily distinct), at least one is not related to the other via R.

core.definition: Not symmetric; having parts or sides that do not correspond in shape, size or arrangement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MET, the third syllable, and the second syllable is a weak uh, so say ay-suh-MEH-trik rather than ay-SIM-et-rik. The middle s is pronounced as s, not as sigh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes structure or design without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In American technical work, asymmetric is common in math, engineering and computing, as in asymmetric encryption or asymmetric data distribution. In everyday speech Americans usually say asymmetrical. The two words overlap, but asymmetric is the preferred form in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly interchangeable, but asymmetric is preferred in technical fields and fixed terms, while asymmetrical is more common in everyday writing.
Unbalanced describes uneven weight or distribution; asymmetric refers specifically to parts that do not match on opposite sides.

examples.everyday: Your haircut looks a little asymmetric, is that on purpose?
examples.professional: We need asymmetric encryption so the public key can be shared without exposing the private key.
examples.analytical: The model shows asymmetric effects, so a shock to one variable does not move the others equally.

nuance.analogy: Like a face where the left and right halves do not mirror each other.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a- not plus symmetria, proportion or agreement in measure.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as asymetric and dropping the m from symmetry
Stressing the wrong syllable as AY-suh-meh-trik or ay-SIM-uh-trik

senses.definition: A self-taught person.
senses.example: Leonardo Da Vinci is one of the greatest autodidacts.

core.definition: A person who has taught themselves a subject or skill without formal schooling or a teacher.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on DYE, and the final syllable is a short 'dakt' with the vowel of 'cat', not a long 'ay'. The middle syllable 'tuh' is reduced to a quick schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually praises someone for learning independently and being intellectually self-reliant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word to describe people who learned a field on their own, often with admiration. In everyday conversation people usually say 'self-taught' instead, and 'autodidact' sounds literary or academic. It works well in writing, speeches, or a thoughtful compliment about someone's knowledge.

distinctions.note: Self-taught is the everyday, neutral phrase and can describe a skill; autodidact is a more formal noun for the person.
Amateur refers to not being paid or professionally trained, while autodidact refers only to how the knowledge was acquired.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is an autodidact; he learned plumbing and basic electrical work entirely from videos.
examples.professional: Our lead engineer is an autodidact who never took a computer science class but writes excellent code.
examples.analytical: Franklin is often described as an autodidact, though his learning depended heavily on books, print networks, and informal mentors.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who learns the trail by walking it alone, with no guide and no map drawn by anyone else.
nuance.etymology: From Greek autodidaktos, 'taught by oneself', from auto- 'self' and didaktos 'taught'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable with a long A, as 'dye-DAYKT'; the ending is a short 'dakt'.
Using 'autodidact' as an adjective; the adjective form is autodidactic.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being avaricious.

core.definition: The quality of being extremely greedy for money, property, or wealth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress stays on RISH, the same syllable as in avaricious. The final -ness is a weak 'nuss' sound with a quick schwa, not a full 'nes' as in 'best'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a moral flaw, usually in a criticizing way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use avariciousness. They usually say avarice or greed, and avariciousness sounds heavy and old-fashioned in conversation. It belongs in essays, reviews, or formal criticism.

distinctions.note: Avarice is the more common noun for the same idea. Avariciousness is a longer, less frequent form that describes the quality of a person or group.
Greed is the everyday term. Avariciousness is more formal and can sound like a trait listed in a character analysis.

examples.everyday: I can't stand the avariciousness of some people at the office who always grab the best seat.
examples.professional: The avariciousness of the vendor's pricing model made the procurement team reconsider the whole contract.
examples.analytical: The novel traces how the avariciousness of the merchant class corrodes civic life and personal loyalty.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that burns more the more you feed it: the appetite grows instead of being satisfied.
nuance.etymology: From avaricious plus the suffix -ness, meaning the quality or state of being.
common_mistakes: Using avariciousness as a verb or adjective; it is only a noun.
Stressing the last syllable: av-uh-RISH-us-ness, not av-uh-rish-us-NESS.

senses.definition: Of or relating to value theory, the philosophical field of axiology.
Of or relating to values themselves.

core.definition: Relating to axiology, the philosophical study of value, including what things are good, right, beautiful or worth having.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the fourth syllable, LAH, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The o is an open AH in General American, and the x is pronounced ks, not gz.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a field of thought without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use axiological almost only in philosophy, ethics, sociology and religious studies. Outside academic writing people say about values or value-based. Use the word in a seminar or paper, but in a meeting say what we value.

distinctions.note: Ethical concerns right and wrong conduct, while axiological covers value more broadly, including aesthetic and non-moral goods.
Normative concerns what we ought to do or believe; axiological concerns what is valuable as such.
Aesthetic concerns beauty and art, which is one kind of value; axiological is the wider category.

examples.everyday: Our argument wasn't really about the numbers; it was about what we think matters, which is an axiological question.
examples.professional: Before we rank the features, we need an axiological decision about which user harms count most.
examples.analytical: Moore's open-question argument is axiological in its concern with whether goodness can be defined in natural terms.

nuance.analogy: Like a ruler that measures the worth of things rather than their length.
nuance.etymology: From Greek axia, worth or value, plus -logical, from logos, study or reason.
common_mistakes: Confusing axiological with axiomatic, which means self-evident or based on axioms.
Stressing the first syllable as in AK-see-uh-LOJ-ih-kul instead of the fourth syllable.

senses.definition: A formula in the language of an axiomatic system, in which one or more schematic variables appear, which stand for any term or subformula of the system, which may or may not be required to satisfy certain conditions.

core.definition: A formula pattern in an axiomatic system whose schematic variables stand for any term or subformula, generating many specific axioms.

pronunciation.tip: Give the strongest stress to SKEE in 'schema' and a lighter secondary stress to AK in 'axiom'. The 'sch' is a plain 'sk' sound, and the final vowel is a soft uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a purely technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Logicians, mathematicians, and computer scientists use this term when discussing formal systems such as set theory or Peano arithmetic. Outside those fields, people will not recognize it, so use it only with an audience that knows logic. Americans usually form the plural as 'schemata' or 'schemas'.

distinctions.note: An axiom is one assumed statement, while an axiom schema is a template that produces many axioms, one for each formula that fits the pattern.
A theorem is proven from axioms, but an axiom schema is assumed and is not proven.

collocations: infinitely many instances of an axiom schema

examples.everyday: I was reading about set theory, and the axiom schema of separation kind of blew my mind.
examples.professional: The Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms include an axiom schema of replacement, so we have to check that our formula qualifies before we use it in the proof.
examples.analytical: Because the induction axiom schema quantifies over all formulas, it cannot be captured by a single first-order axiom.

nuance.analogy: Like a cookie cutter: one shape stamps out many cookies, and each cookie is one axiom.
nuance.etymology: From Greek axioma, 'that which is thought fit', and skhema, 'form, shape'.
common_mistakes: Calling a single axiom an axiom schema, when the schema is a template that generates many axioms.
Using 'schema' as a singular for the plural form; the plural is schemata or schemas.

senses.definition: A large wagon used to carry a band of musicians in a parade.
A current movement that attracts wide support.
To join a bandwagon (a current movement that attracts wide support).

core.definition: A popular movement or trend that many people join, often because others are joining rather than from deep conviction.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'BAND' with a weaker secondary stress on 'wag'. The final syllable is a reduced 'uhn', not 'ahn' as in French.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests people are following a trend for social or opportunistic reasons rather than from conviction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'jump on the bandwagon' or 'climb on the bandwagon' when someone joins a popular cause late, especially in politics, sports, or business. It is common in news commentary and everyday talk. Saying it about your own choice can sound self-deprecating; saying it about others sounds slightly critical. The phrase is idiomatic, so don't translate it literally.

distinctions.note: A trend is neutral and describes a direction of change; a bandwagon emphasizes people joining a movement because others already have.
A fad is a short-lived craze; a bandwagon is the social process of joining, whether the movement lasts or not.

examples.everyday: Half my friends suddenly love pickleball, so I guess I'm jumping on the bandwagon too.
examples.professional: Several vendors have jumped on the bandwagon and added AI features, but few have real use cases yet.
examples.analytical: Public opinion can form a bandwagon effect in which people adopt a position simply because it appears popular.

nuance.analogy: A bandwagon is like a parade float: people climb aboard to be part of the celebration, whether or not they know where it is going.
nuance.etymology: From bandwagon, a wagon carrying a band in a parade, which by the 19th century was used figuratively for a popular movement.
common_mistakes: Using 'bandwagon' as a general word for any group or team, without the sense of joining a popular trend.
Using the preposition 'in' instead of 'on' with 'jump on the bandwagon'.
Thinking the word is a verb in all uses; 'bandwagon' is mainly a noun, with 'jump on the bandwagon' as the verbal phrase.

senses.definition: A Christian sacrament, by which one is received into a church and sometimes given a name, generally involving the candidate to be anointed with or submerged in water.
senses.example: The child’s baptism was held at the old church.

senses.definition: A similar ceremony of initiation, purification or naming.
The moment at which an object is first assigned a proper name.

core.definition: The Christian rite of washing with or immersion in water that marks entry into the church and union with Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'BAP.' The 's' is pronounced /z/, and the ending is a weak 'um.' Do not say 'bap-TEEZ-um.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and solemn in Christian contexts; 'baptism by fire' or 'baptism of fire' is a figurative expression for a hard first experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'get baptized,' 'be baptized,' or 'have a baptism.' It is a major event in church life, often with a family gathering afterward. Figuratively, 'baptism of fire' means a difficult first test.

distinctions.note: Christening usually means the baptism of an infant with the giving of a name, and is more informal and traditional.
Confirmation is a separate rite that affirms baptismal faith, especially in Catholic and Anglican churches.
Immersion is one mode of baptism, in which the person is fully submerged.

examples.everyday: We're having my nephew's baptism at church this Sunday, and then lunch at my sister's house.
examples.professional: Our pastor schedules baptism classes for adults before each spring baptism service.
examples.analytical: Paul interprets baptism as participation in Christ's death and resurrection, not merely a ritual of cleansing.

nuance.analogy: Baptism is like a public passage through water, marking where a new life with Christ begins.
nuance.etymology: From Greek baptisma, from baptizein, 'to dip, immerse.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 's' as /s/ instead of /z/.
Using 'baptism' and 'baptist' interchangeably; the second names a person or denomination.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek baptisma comes from baptizo, 'to immerse.' Matthew 3:13-17 tells of Jesus baptized by John in the Jordan. Matthew 28:19 has the risen Christ command disciples to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Romans 6:3-4 teaches that those baptized share in Christ's death and new life.

traditions.view: Baptism is a sacrament of full threefold immersion, given to infants and adults, and is immediately followed by chrismation and Communion.
Baptism is a sacrament that removes original sin and incorporates a person into the Church. It is usually given to infants by pouring or immersion, and is followed by confirmation and Eucharist.

Lutherans, Anglicans, and Reformed baptize infants and see baptism as a means of grace or covenant sign. Baptists and Pentecostals practice believer's baptism by immersion and treat it as an ordinance witnessing to faith.

baptism.etymology: From Middle English *bapteme*, *baptesme*, from Old French *batesme* or *bapteme*, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin *baptisma*, from Ancient Greek *βάπτισμα* (“dipping, baptism”), from *βαπτίζω* (“I dip in liquid”).

senses.definition: Supporting or pertaining to the theologian Barlaam of Seminara, especially his opposition to Hesychasm.
An advocate of Barlaamite views, an opponent of Hesychasm.

core.definition: Relating to Barlaam of Seminara and his fourteenth-century opposition to Hesychasm, the Byzantine practice of contemplative prayer.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LAH, the third syllable of the four. The ending -ite is pronounced like mite, and the middle syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a historical position in a theological debate rather than attacking a person.
nuance.usage_note: Barlaamite appears in scholarly work on Byzantine theology and Eastern Orthodox history, in seminary courses and academic books. Americans rarely use it outside those settings. In everyday or church conversation, people would more likely say followers of Barlaam or Barlaam's view.

distinctions.note: A Hesychast practices the prayer of stillness; a Barlaamite opposed that practice and its theology.
A Palamite followed Gregory Palamas, who defended Hesychasm against Barlaam, so the two groups are opponents in this debate.

examples.everyday: At the seminary dinner, a professor mentioned a Barlaamite view, and I had to look it up later.
examples.professional: The course syllabus includes a Barlaamite critique of the Hesychast prayer tradition.
examples.analytical: Barlaamite critics argued that the Hesychast claim to see the divine light could not be reconciled with the unknowability of God's essence, a point at the center of the dispute.

nuance.analogy: A Barlaamite is like an examiner who doubts the methods a mystic claims to use.
nuance.etymology: From the name Barlaam of Seminara, with the suffix -ite.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in BAR-la-mite, instead of bahr-LAH-uh-mite.
Using Barlaamite as a general word for any critic of mysticism; it refers to Barlaam and his specific position.

senses.definition: A directed acyclic graph whose vertices represent random variables and whose directed edges represent conditional dependencies. Each random variable can fall into any of at least two mutually disjoint states, and has a probability function which takes as inputs the states of its parent nodes and returns as output the probability of being in a certain state for a given combination of the states of its parent nodes. A node without parent nodes just has an unconditioned probability of being in some given state.

core.definition: A graph of variables linked by conditional dependencies, used to compute probabilities and reason under uncertainty.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NET, the first syllable of network, while BAY-zee-un keeps a lighter stress. Network ends in an r-colored vowel, so say 'wurk', not 'wok'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term used in professional and research settings.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and AI engineers say Bayesian network in technical meetings, and specialists often shorten it to 'Bayes net'. For nontechnical listeners, explain it as a map showing which factors influence which others. You may hear 'Bayes net' casually in team chat, so it is worth knowing both forms.

distinctions.note: A neural network learns patterns through layers of weights and is hard to interpret, while a Bayesian network encodes explicit probabilistic relationships among variables that you can read.
A decision tree splits data into branches for classification, while a Bayesian network models probabilities among many interrelated variables.

examples.everyday: My friend who works at a bank says their fraud system is built on a Bayesian network, which sounds fancy but is basically a map of what causes what.
examples.professional: We built the churn model as a Bayesian network so the product team can see how pricing and support tickets affect cancellations.
examples.analytical: A Bayesian network encodes probabilistic structure in a directed acyclic graph, so the factorization of the joint distribution follows directly from the graph's edges.

nuance.analogy: It's like a family tree of probabilities: each node depends on its parents, and learning about a parent changes what you expect of the child.
nuance.etymology: Bayesian comes from Thomas Bayes; network combines net and work, meaning an interlaced structure.
common_mistakes: Confusing a Bayesian network with a neural network; they serve different purposes and differ in interpretability.
Saying 'bay-ZHEE-un' with a strong stress on the middle syllable; keep the stress on NET in the full term.

bayesian-network.etymology: Named after Thomas Bayes (1701–1761), English mathematician.

conversation.text: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph where each node has a probability distribution conditioned on its parents.
We built a small Bayesian network to estimate failure risk from maintenance and usage data.
The Bayesian network shows which factors influence each other and by how much.

core.definition: A name of several kings of Aram (Syria) in the Old Testament, who fought against Israel and Judah in the 9th and 8th centuries BC.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, HAY, which is the most prominent sound. The final syllable is a weak "dad" with a short vowel, not a long one.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name used in Bible study, sermons and religious history. Capitalize it, and say "Ben-HAY-dad" even though Americans may also say "Ben-hah-DAD" in Bible class.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group was reading about a king named Ben-hadad who kept fighting against Israel.
examples.professional: In my lesson on the divided monarchy, I introduced Ben-hadad as the Aramean king who repeatedly threatened Ahab's Israel.
examples.analytical: The narrative of 1 Kings 20 presents Ben-hadad as a proud foreign ruler whose military overconfidence sets up the prophetic defeat of Aram.

nuance.analogy: Like a title passed down a royal line, Ben-hadad names a dynasty of Syrian kings rather than just one man.
nuance.etymology: Means "son of Hadad," Hadad being the name of a Syrian storm god.
common_mistakes: Saying the name as one word without the hyphen-like pause between Ben and Hadad.
Confusing the Ben-hadad kings with the nation of Aram itself.
nuance.biblical_note: Ben-hadad was the title of several kings of Aram (Syria), with Damascus as their capital. Ben-hadad I, son of Tabrimmon, made a treaty with Asa of Judah against Baasha of Israel in 1 Kings 15:18. In 1 Kings 20:1 Ben-hadad besieged Samaria, and God gave Israel victory through a prophet. In 2 Kings 6:24 another Ben-hadad besieged Samaria so severely that famine followed.

senses.definition: A brief, often minimalistic two-piece bathing suit worn by women, especially one that exposes the midriff and navel.
A brief bathing suit covering only the pelvis (equivalent to the bottom portion of a two-piece bikini), worn by any gender.
Brief underpants or trousers that reach to the hips rather than the waist and have high cut leg holes.

core.definition: A women's two-piece swimsuit with a separate top and bottom, usually leaving the midriff exposed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KEE. The first syllable is a reduced bih, so avoid saying bee-KEE-nee with a long first vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts, though it can carry a revealing or suggestive tone depending on how it is described.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bikini for any two-piece suit, and one-piece for a single-piece suit. The word is common in shopping and beach talk, as in I'm looking for a bikini top. Swimsuit is the general and most polite term, while bikini is more specific and casual.

distinctions.note: A one-piece is a single suit covering the torso and legs, while a bikini has two separate pieces.
A tankini has a longer tank-style top that covers more of the midriff than a bikini top does.

examples.everyday: I'll grab a towel and my bikini, and we can head to the lake this afternoon.
examples.professional: Our buyers want more bikini options in the summer line before we finalize the orders next week.
examples.analytical: The bikini, as a fashion category, reflects shifting social norms about the public display of the body across the twentieth century.

nuance.analogy: A bikini is like a dress split in half, where the top and bottom are separate pieces that meet only at your skin.
nuance.etymology: Named after Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands, where the United States tested atomic bombs in 1946.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in BIH-kee-nee; the stress is on the second syllable.
Using bikini as a generic word for all swimsuits; swimsuit or one-piece is more general, and bikini specifically means two pieces.

bikini.etymology: From French *bikini*, named after the place name *Bikini*, the name of the atoll where the United States tested nuclear weapons in July 1946; it was reckoned that the bathing suit would cause as much excitement as a nuclear bomb.

conversation.text: She bought a new bikini for spring break.
I don't really wear bikinis; I prefer a one-piece.
Is that bikini top too small, or is it supposed to fit like that?

senses.definition: A short informal letter.
A written order to quarter soldiers.
A sealed ticket for a draw or lottery.
A place where a soldier is assigned to lodge.
Temporary lodgings in a private residence, such as is organized for members of a visiting sports team.
An allocated space or berth in a boat or ship.
Berth; position.
A semi-finished length of metal.
A short piece of wood, especially one used as firewood.
A short cutting of sugar cane produced by a harvester or used for planting.
A rectangle used as a charge on an escutcheon.
An ornament in Norman work, resembling a billet of wood, either square or round.
A strap that enters a buckle.
A loop that receives the end of a buckled strap.
To lodge soldiers, or guests, usually by order.
To lodge, or be quartered, in a private house.
To direct, by a ticket or note, where to lodge.

core.definition: A place to stay, especially a room or house assigned to soldiers, or a military job position assigned to a person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final -et sound like 'it', not like the French 'bee-YAY'. The middle syllable is short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In military contexts it is a plain, practical term.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans meet billet in history books, military news or talk about the armed forces. Military personnel use it to mean a job slot, as in 'He has a billet on the staff.' Civilians rarely use it for a room, except when discussing historical soldier housing. In everyday speech, 'lodging' or 'a place to stay' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Barracks are buildings built specifically to house soldiers, while a billet is any place, often a private home, where soldiers are assigned to stay.
Quarters is a broader word for any housing, while billet suggests an official assignment to lodge soldiers or staff.

examples.everyday: My grandfather said his unit was billeted in a farmhouse during the winter.
examples.professional: The new analyst position is a billet in the operations group, so it comes with a clear command structure.
examples.analytical: The historical practice of billeting troops in private homes raised deep questions about property, consent and state power.

nuance.analogy: A billet is like a reserved seat on a bus: it has been assigned to you, and you are expected to occupy it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French billette, 'small log or note', related to bille, 'log'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'lay', like the French 'billet-AY'.
Confusing billet with 'bullet' because the spelling and sound are similar.

billet.etymology: From Middle English *bylet*, from Anglo-Norman *billette* (“list, schedule”), from *bille* + *ette*, from Latin *bulla* (“document”).

senses.definition: To divide an angle, line segment, or other figure into two equal parts.
To cut or divide into two parts.
senses.example: The river bisects the town.

senses.definition: To perform a binary search on files in source control in order to identify the specific change that introduced a bug etc.
A bisector, which divides into two equal parts.

An envelope, card, or fragment thereof showing an affixed cut half of a regular issued stamp, over which one or more postal markings have been applied. Typically used in wartime when normal lower rate stamps may not be available.

core.definition: To divide a line, angle, or other figure into two equal parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable: bye-SEKT, not BY-sekt. Don't add a vowel before the final -ct; it is just a k sound followed by a t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise technical verb with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bisect mainly in geometry classes, engineering, and software development, where git bisect is a standard debugging command. In everyday speech people say cut in half or split in half instead. Outside math and technical talk, bisect sounds stiff, so use it when precision matters.

distinctions.note: Dissect means to cut apart in order to examine in detail, and the parts need not be equal; bisect means dividing into two equal halves.
Halve is the everyday word for cutting something into two equal parts; bisect is more technical and geometric.

collocations: run git bisect to find the bug

examples.everyday: My son asked me how to bisect a right angle with just a ruler and a compass.
examples.professional: I'll run git bisect on the commit history to find which change broke the build.
examples.analytical: A line that bisects a segment at right angles is called the perpendicular bisector.

nuance.analogy: Like folding a sheet of paper exactly in half along a crease.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bi- 'two' plus secare 'to cut'.
common_mistakes: Confusing bisect with dissect, which means to cut apart for close examination, not into equal halves.
Misspelling it as 'bissect'; the correct spelling is bisect.
Stressing the first syllable, as in BY-sekt.

senses.definition: Without color; pale; pallid.
Desolate and exposed; swept by cold winds.
senses.example: a bleak and bare rock

senses.definition: Unhappy; cheerless; miserable; emotionally desolate.
senses.example: Downtown Albany felt bleak that February after the divorce.

senses.definition: A small European river fish (Alburnus alburnus), of the family Cyprinidae.

core.definition: Cold, bare and empty, or without hope, comfort or cheerful feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the vowel long and tense, like the ee in seek; don't say blick. The final k is lightly unreleased before a pause.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes harsh, empty or hopeless conditions or outlooks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bleak for weather, landscapes, business prospects and news, as in a bleak winter or a bleak outlook. It is common in both speech and writing. In casual talk people might say grim or gloomy, but bleak suggests a more lasting lack of hope.

distinctions.note: Gloomy describes a dark mood or dim place; bleak adds a sense of desolation and lack of any hope for improvement.
Grim suggests serious, harsh or frightening conditions; bleak emphasizes emptiness and lack of promise.
Dreary describes something dull and tiresome; bleak is stronger and implies hopelessness or exposure.

examples.everyday: The forecast for this weekend looks pretty bleak, with rain and cold wind all day.
examples.professional: The sales forecast looks bleak for the next two quarters unless we win the new contract.
examples.analytical: Camus presents a bleak vision of human existence, yet he insists that one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

nuance.analogy: Like a winter field with no leaves or color: nothing is growing, and nothing seems likely to.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blāc, meaning pale or shining; the meaning shifted toward bare and desolate.
common_mistakes: Using bleak to mean just sad for a short time; it suggests a more hopeless, lasting condition.
Pronouncing the vowel as a short i, as in black or blick.

bleak.etymology: From Middle English *bleke* (also *bleche*, whence the English doublet ), and *bleike*, and earlier Middle English *blak*, *blac* (“pale, wan”), from Old English *blǣc*, *blǣċ*, *blāc* (“bleak, pale, pallid”) and Old Norse *bleikr* (“pale, whitish”), all…

senses.definition: A small variety of surfboard, often made of foam; a bodyboard.
To travel by boogieboard.

core.definition: A short, lightweight surfboard, often made of foam or plastic, that you ride lying down or kneeling.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have a primary stress: the first word is secondary and the second word is primary. The word board ends with a clear rhotic r, and the word boogie sounds like 'BOO-gee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests beach fun, summer vacations and casual surfing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say boogie board at the beach to mean the small foam body board that kids and casual surfers use. The term is also written as boogieboard or body board. Lifeguards and beach shops use the same name, so it is easy to say on a vacation.

distinctions.note: A surfboard is usually longer and stand-up, while a boogie board is shorter and ridden lying down or kneeling.
Bodyboard is the more general term; boogie board is a brand-based name that Americans use for the same type of board.

examples.everyday: We rented two boogie boards from the shop on the boardwalk for the kids.
examples.professional: Our outdoor recreation team sells boogie boards alongside kayaks and beach gear.
examples.analytical: The boogie board's simplicity reflects a democratic form of surfing that asks little skill of the rider.

nuance.analogy: Like a small raft that carries you into the waves, a boogie board lets you ride the surf without standing up.
common_mistakes: Saying 'boogie-bored' or stressing the second word too strongly; the stress is on both words, with board weighted slightly more.
Using surfboard for a boogie board, which can confuse people at a beach rental shop.

conversation.text: The kids rode their boogie boards all afternoon.
A boogie board is a lot easier than a surfboard for beginners.
Let's pick up a cheap boogie board at the store by the beach.

senses.definition: A dish (usually meat) prepared by braising.
senses.example: Pot roast is typically a braise, as is osso buco.

senses.definition: A sauce used for braising.
senses.example: Braised cabbage is cooked in a braise of sliced bacon, one or two thickly sliced onions, one or two sliced carrots, parsley, thyme, a bay leaf, and stock to nearly cover.

senses.definition: Pagellus bogaraveo, syn. Pagellus centrodontus (sea bream)
To cook in a small amount of liquid, in a covered pan, somewhere between steaming and boiling.

core.definition: To cook meat or vegetables slowly in a small amount of liquid inside a covered pot, so they become tender.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable that rhymes with 'days,' and the ending is a clear z sound. Non-native speakers often add a vowel after the r or say 'brah-zee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. The word suggests patient, comforting home cooking, and it is common in restaurant menus and cookbooks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use braise mostly for cooking tough cuts like short ribs, lamb shanks, or pork shoulder, and for hearty greens. You will see 'braised' on menus far more often than you will hear 'braise' in casual talk. If you are at a restaurant and ask what a dish is, 'It's braised in red wine' is a natural answer.

distinctions.note: Roasting cooks food with dry heat in an oven, while braising uses a small amount of liquid and a covered pot.
A stew is usually made from small pieces of meat cooked in plenty of liquid, while a braise is often a larger cut cooked in less liquid.

examples.everyday: I'm making those braised short ribs you liked, so come over around six.
examples.professional: The restaurant's chef said the braised pork shoulder can be prepped the day before and reheated for service.
examples.analytical: Braising transforms collagen-rich connective tissue into gelatin, which is why a tough cut becomes silky after several hours in the pot.

nuance.analogy: Think of a slow cooker on the stove: the lid traps moisture, so the meat softens gently instead of drying out.
nuance.etymology: From French braiser, from braise 'hot embers,' from a Germanic root related to the idea of burning.
common_mistakes: Confusing braise with braze, a homophone that means joining metal with a filler metal.
Pronouncing it with an extra syllable, such as 'brah-zee' or 'bray-ZAY'.

braise.etymology: From French *braise* (“live coals”) and *braiser* (“to braise”, from the noun), from Old French *brese* (“embers”), from Old Low Franconian/; akin to /, Norwegian/Swedish dialectal *brasa* (“to roast”), Danish dialectal *brase* (“to flambé, enflame”).

conversation.text: Braise the short ribs for three hours.
I like to braise chicken thighs with wine.
The braised beef was so tender.

senses.definition: A kind of statistical score meant to gauge the accuracy of probabilistic predictions more precisely than simple calibration.

core.definition: A statistical measure of the accuracy of probability forecasts, computed as the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual binary outcomes.

pronunciation.tip: Brier is named for meteorologist Glenn Brier, so say BRY-er, with the final syllable reduced to 'er'. Keep the r in 'score' rhotic and stress 'score' as the main stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term that signals expertise in forecasting or statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Brier score in meteorology, machine learning, forecasting, and statistics, mostly in technical reports, papers, and model evaluation discussions. Outside those fields, people would not use it. In a work meeting, you might say 'our Brier score improved after recalibration' to a team of data scientists.

distinctions.note: Log loss punishes confident wrong predictions very heavily, while the Brier score penalizes errors more gently and is bounded.
Calibration describes whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, while the Brier score is a single number that combines calibration and resolution.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in weather forecasting says her Brier score is the number her boss actually checks.
examples.professional: After we recalibrated the classifier, our Brier score dropped from 0.21 to 0.16 on the holdout set.
examples.analytical: The Brier score rewards honest probability estimates, so a forecaster cannot game it by hedging toward fifty percent.

nuance.analogy: The Brier score is like a golf score for forecasts: lower is better, and every miss adds strokes.
nuance.etymology: Named after Glenn W. Brier, the American meteorologist who proposed it in 1950.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with a classification accuracy score; the Brier score uses probabilities, not just right or wrong answers.
Saying 'Bryer' with a long i and extra vowel, instead of the standard BRY-er.
Thinking higher is better; a lower Brier score means more accurate forecasts.

senses.definition: All the guns on one side of a warship.
The simultaneous firing of these guns.
A forceful attack, whether written or spoken.
